default.p.chokuzen_n3-t61-p1.vietnamese:
「No Time」
We often say, “I don’t have time.”
But do we really have “no time”?
In fact, there may be times when we pretend to be busy even though we have time, or put ourselves into a state of being busy.
For example, something like this happened to me.
A few days ago, I took the train to work.
Because I was in a hurry, I forgot everything from my mobile phone and music player to my book.
Normally, as soon as I get on the train, I put earphones in my ears, take a book or newspaper out of my bag, and sit down to read.
Sometimes I also start playing a game on my mobile phone or handheld game console.
But that day, since I had boarded the train without bringing anything, I had nothing to do.
With no other option, I spent the entire ride doing nothing but watching the movements of the person sitting in the seat in front of me and looking out the window.
After doing that, I was able to relax very comfortably.
As this shows, perhaps we also need periods when we do nothing.
I feel that we deliberately create unnecessary things to do and make our lives busy.
Wouldn’t we be able to regain more meaningful and fulfilling periods of time simply by trying to consider whether we really “have no time”?

default.p.chokuzen_n3-t66-p1.vietnamese:
A New-Style Magazine
The magazine「Japan Lifestyle」, which introduces the lives of people from overseas who live in Japan, has been released at bookstores nationwide.
Until now, newspapers and magazines have occasionally provided brief introductions to international students living in Japan and foreigners working in Japan, but it is extremely rare for a magazine centered on their everyday lives to be published.
The magazine’s cover design is also bright and looks very interesting.
The magazine uses many colorful photographs and illustrations to vividly introduce their living conditions.
This magazine is not published monthly but quarterly, meaning it is scheduled to be published four times a year—in spring, summer, autumn, and winter.
Until now, the magazine had been sold by mail only to readers who had placed advance orders online, but sales were better than expected, and for that reason it was decided that the magazine would also be sold at bookstores.
The publisher says: 「Through this magazine, we hope that foreign residents can listen to and share one another’s worries and joys, so that their lives in Japan will become even a little better」.
The publisher also reportedly plans to continue introducing information about exchange events with Japanese people held throughout Japan.

default.p.chokuzen_n3-t67-p1.vietnamese:
Food and Communication
Have you ever heard the saying 「The way to a man's heart is through his stomach」?
You may have heard someone say this while discussing romantic matters or asking for relationship advice.
Men tend to like women who cook delicious food for them; in other words, meals are very important to men.
However, this saying does not apply only to love or to men.
That is because food plays an extremely important role in communication between people.
For example, if you want to become closer to someone, do you not feel that inviting them by saying 「Let's go eat some delicious sweets together」 would make it much easier for the two of you to become close than saying 「Shall we go for a walk nearby?」?
In fact, I am sure you also have memories of becoming much closer to someone after eating and drinking together.
The important role of meals is not limited to making friends or finding a boyfriend or girlfriend.
Even when discussing business, sharing a meal has great significance.
Knowing restaurants with good service and food, where people can talk calmly and comfortably, can even become an effective way to help business discussions proceed smoothly.

default.p.chokuzen_n3-t71-p1.vietnamese:
Signs of Autumn
Speaking of late August, it is still a very hot time of year.
The sun shines intensely, and people walking on the city’s asphalt are exhausted by the heat.
It is hot every day, and many people probably lose their energy as a result.
However, if you go into the mountains and forests, you will notice that the air is cooler than in the city and that signs of autumn soon fill the area.

Remember that「中間」uses 中, meaning the middle, whereas「仲間」uses 仲, referring to human relationships. It can also follow another noun to indicate a group of people in the same field, as in: 「高校時代のサッカー仲間と今でも連絡を取り合っている。」(I still keep in touch with my soccer teammates from high school.)

Distinguish「肌」(はだ) from「皮膚」(ひふ):「ひふ」is an academic medical term for biological structure or disease, while「はだ」has a more personal and aesthetic nuance. default.q.chokuzen_n3-t30-q10.explanation: 「集中」(しゅうちゅう) is a noun and group 3 verb meaning to direct all one's mind, energy, or attention toward a specific object. It commonly takes に in the pattern「〜に集中する」. The complete sentence means: "Turn off the TV so you can concentrate fully on your studies." Another familiar example is:「周りの音が気にならず、読書に集中できた。」(I was able to concentrate on reading without being distracted by the surrounding noise.) To avoid confusion: use「集中」for directing one's thoughts or attention,「収集」for gathering or collecting objects, and「募集」for recruiting people to participate.

default.q.chokuzen_n3-t31-q11.explanation: The word「ヒント」(from the English word “hint”) means “a clue,” “a suggestion,” or “a helpful tip.” It is used when someone is stuck on a problem, puzzle, or difficult situation and needs a small clue to find a solution independently. It commonly appears in expressions such as ヒントを出す/与える, ヒントを得る, and ヒントにする. The complete translation of sentence (d) is: "This question is too difficult, so could you please give me some hints so I can solve it?" To distinguish it from similar loanwords, remember that JLPT questions may use「ピント」(the camera’s focus, choice (a)) or「ポイント」(accumulated shopping points, choice (c)) as traps.「ヒント」is associated with finding the solution to a question or problem (解く, 答える). Contrastive example:「先生が出してくれたヒントのおかげで、難しいパズルが解けた。」(Thanks to the hint the teacher gave me, I was able to solve the difficult puzzle.)

It describes something troublesome that obstructs space or a passage, or someone’s actions that bother others. In sentence (b), it correctly describes a large rock taking up space on the road and blocking traffic: “Because there is a large rock in the road, it is obstructing the way.” Another common example is: 「仕事の邪魔をしないでください。」(Please do not interfere with my work.) To avoid the trap, remember that 「じゃま」does not evaluate abstract qualities such as personality or the difficulty of a book; it is associated with concrete obstruction of space or an activity.

default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q11.explanation: The noun「相手」(あいて) refers to the other person or party involved in a two-way interaction such as conversation, competition, work, or marriage. Another typical example is:「彼はテニスのいい練習相手だ。」(He is a good tennis practice partner.)「相手」must be an interactive counterpart, so (a) and (d), which refer to objects or food, can be eliminated, as can (b), which refers to a random pedestrian without a corresponding interaction.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q11.why.0: ✗ (a) 「相手」is used for a person or organization involved in an interaction, not for objects that go together; for a table and chairs, use セット.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q11.why.1: ✗ (b) To refer generally to people walking in a park, use 人 or 人々; 「相手」is inappropriate when there is no specific interacting party.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q11.why.2: ✓ (c) 「電話の相手」is a natural and correct expression for the person on the other end of the telephone call.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q11.why.3: ✗ (d) Food eaten together with rice is usually called おかず or お供; the noun 「相手」 is not used for food or drinks.

Be careful not to confuse 「おしゃれ」(fashionable) with 「おしゃべり」(chatty or talkative), as in sentence (d).
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q2.why.0: ✗ (a) When describing a room that has just been cleaned, an adjective indicating cleanliness such as 「きれい」 must be used; a word meaning “fashionable,” such as 「おしゃれ」, is not appropriate.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q2.why.1: ✗ (b) The contrasting clause needs a word describing a personality flaw, such as 「へん」or 「だらしない」, rather than a positive word meaning “fashionable,” such as 「おしゃれ」.

「力を試す（ためす）」is a natural expression meaning to test one's ability or skills.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q3.explanation: The transitive verb「試す（ためす）」takes the particle を and means carrying out a concrete action to test quality, function, or actual ability. Sentence (d) means: "I intend to take the exam to test how good my Japanese is." In daily conversation, it is common in situations involving trial or experience, such as「新しい靴の履き心地を試してみる。」(I will try on the new shoes to see how comfortable they are.) Do not confuse「ためす」(to test or try out) with the similar-sounding「ためる」(貯める; to save up money in choice (b)) or「たしかめる」(確かめる; to verify information in choice (a)).
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q3.why.0: ✗ (a) To express looking at a clock to check or confirm the time, Japanese uses the verbs 確認した or 確かめた, not ためした.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q3.why.1: ✗ (b) When talking about accumulating or saving money to build a house, the correct form is ためて（貯めて）, not the verb ためして.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q3.why.2: ✗ (c) To express repairing an old bicycle so that it can continue to be used, use 修理して or 直して instead of ためして.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q3.why.3: ✓ (d) The verb ためす correctly combines in the phrase 力をためす to express testing one's ability or checking one's Japanese proficiency through an exam.

The noun 「アンケート」 combines naturally with the verb 「取る」 in the expression 「アンケートを取る」, meaning to collect survey responses from everyone.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q4.explanation: The word 「アンケート」(from the French enquête) means a questionnaire or opinion survey conducted to collect data and views from a group. In Japanese, it commonly appears in collocations such as 「アンケートを取る/行う」(conduct a survey) when you are collecting the data, and 「アンケートに答える」(answer a survey) when you are responding as a participant. The complete sentence (d) means: "We collected survey responses from all the class members before deciding how to proceed." Another example is: 「新商品の開発に向けて、街頭でアンケートを行った。」(We conducted a street survey for the development of a new product.) To remember it, do not confuse 「アンケート」(survey) with the similarly sounding katakana word 「アンコール」(encore), as in option (a), which refers to a request for another performance at a concert.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q4.why.0: ✗ (a) When an enthusiastic audience applauds and asks an artist to perform again at the end of a concert, the correct word is 「アンコール」(encore), not 「アンケート」.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q4.why.1: ✗ (b) When completing a survey form, the expression 「アンケートに答える」(answer a survey) is used, not 「アンケートに質問した」.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q4.why.2: ✗ (c) To address a lack of exercise, one should invite a friend to exercise or play sports, using words such as 「運動」 or 「スポーツ」, not conduct a survey 「アンケート」.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q4.why.3: ✓ (d) 「アンケートを取る」 is exactly the correct expression for surveying all class members to reach agreement on how to proceed.

The verb 配る (くばる) means to distribute and is used when giving the same type of item or document to multiple people.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q5.explanation: The Group I transitive verb「配る」(くばる) commonly follows the pattern「[large group of recipients] に [object] を配る」. It means distributing documents, flyers, or goods evenly to many people within a specific group or area. Therefore, sentence (b) means: “Please distribute the exam papers to everyone.” Another practical example:「駅の前でチラシを配っています。」(They are handing out flyers in front of the station.)「配る」must generally target multiple recipients, whereas giving something to one individual requires「渡す」or「あげる」.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q5.why.0: ✗ (a) When paying for a purchase at a cashier, Japanese uses the verb 払う (はらう), not 配る.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q5.why.1: ✓ (b) The verb 配る is used completely correctly to describe distributing the test papers to everyone present.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q5.why.2: ✗ (c) For giving a birthday present to one person, such as your mother, use あげるor 渡す; 配るis used only when distributing something to multiple recipients.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q5.why.3: ✗ (d) To describe a computer running fast or operating smoothly, use 作動が速い. 配る is completely inappropriate in meaning.

「係」(かかり) is correctly used to refer to someone responsible for or assigned to a particular task within a group.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q6.explanation: The noun 「係」（かかり） can stand alone or follow a noun referring to an activity or task. It denotes the person responsible for a specific duty in a classroom or organization. Sentence (a) translates as: “My child was assigned to clean the classroom.” Another example: 「質問がある方は、案内係にお尋ねください。」(If you have any questions, please ask the person in charge of guidance.) Remember that 「係」 refers to an assigned role or duty; it does not describe interpersonal relationships like 「関係」 or a group category like 「仲間」.

The noun-verb 「挑戦」means to take on or try something new or challenging. It correctly combines with the particle in 「〜に挑戦する」.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q7.explanation: The noun 「挑戦」(ちょうせん) refers to courageously taking on a challenge. It commonly takes に in the structure 「[goal/new field] に挑戦する」, expressing the will to test oneself and push beyond one’s limits. Thus, the complete sentence means: "This year, I want to experience and challenge myself in a new field of work." A practical example is: 「来年、JLPT N2の試験に挑戦するつもりです。」(I plan to take on the JLPT N2 exam next year.) Be careful with choice (b): although 挑戦 can suggest challenging someone, ordinary head-to-head competition in sports is expressed with 「試合をする」. 挑戦する is used for a major goal such as breaking a record or challenging for a championship, as in 「記録／チャンピオンに挑戦する」.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q7.why.0: ✓ (a) 「新しい仕事に挑戦する」 naturally expresses the intention to take on a new job.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q7.why.1: ✗ (b) A competitive sports match against an opponent should use「試合」(or「対戦」), not「挑戦」.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q7.why.2: ✗ (c) When expressing an opportunity to interact with and meet people, the correct noun is 「機会」or 「チャンス」.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q7.why.3: ✗ (d) A bad relationship leading to friction and arguments should use「喧嘩」, not「挑戦」.

The verb 「つつむ」（包む）means to wrap an object in paper or cloth, so wrapping the present in attractive paper is exactly the correct usage.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q8.explanation: The verb 「つつむ」(包む), a Group 1 transitive verb, commonly follows the structure 「～を［material］で包む」. Its basic meaning is to wrap an object completely in paper, cloth, or another soft material. It can also be used figuratively for fog, smoke, or an atmosphere enveloping an entire space. The completed sentence in (b) means: "Since this is a gift, please wrap it in nice paper for me." Another example is: 「割れやすいお皿を新聞紙で丁寧に包んで箱に入れた。」 (I carefully wrapped the fragile plate in newspaper and put it in a box.) To avoid confusion on the JLPT, distinguish 「包む」 from tying with rope, 「縛る（しばる）」 in (a), sticking or patching with tape, 「貼る（はる）」 in (c), and covering a surface with falling snow, 「覆う（おおう）」 in (d).
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q8.why.0: ✗ (a) To secure a tent so that the wind does not blow it away, it must be tied down with rope (縛る), not wrapped with「つつむ」(to wrap or cover).
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q8.why.1: ✓ (b) This sentence is completely correct because 「つつむ」describes wrapping a gift in attractive paper.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q8.why.2: ✗ (c) When repairing torn paper with tape, use the verb「はる」(貼る), not「つつむ」.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q8.why.3: ✗ (d) For snow covering the surface of a mountain peak, the verbs「おおう」(覆う) or「つもる」(積もる) must be used; 「つつむ」is incorrect.

The verb「こぼす」means to spill or knock over and is used with liquids or small loose objects. It therefore correctly combines with「コーヒー」(coffee).
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q9.explanation: The verb「こぼす」(零す) is a Group 1 transitive verb used with the particle を in the pattern「[liquid/small particles] をこぼす」. It describes accidentally spilling, pouring out, or scattering liquid or small objects from a container in everyday situations. Accordingly, the complete sentence means: "I accidentally spilled coffee on my shirt, so I immediately went to change into another outfit." To avoid a common trap in this type of question, remember that「こぼす」is used only for liquid or tiny objects spilling out of a container. It is never used for dropping a solid object (use「落とす」as in choices a and b) or for leaving property behind (use「置き忘れる」as in choice c). Compare it with this familiar example:「コップにジュースを注ぎすぎて、机の上にこぼしてしまった。」(I poured too much juice into the glass and accidentally spilled it onto the desk.)
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q9.why.0: ✗ (a) A bag (かばん) is a solid object, so dropping it requires the transitive verb 「落とす」rather than 「こぼす」.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q9.why.1: ✗ (b) When a dropped watch (時計) is damaged after hitting the floor, use「壊して」or「壊れて」, not「こぼして」.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q9.why.2: ✗ (c) For leaving belongings such as a wallet (さいふ) on a train, 「忘れて」or 「置き忘れて」must be used to express the intended meaning.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t32-q9.why.3: ✓ (d)「こぼす」combines correctly with the noun for a liquid,「コーヒー」, to describe accidentally spilling coffee on a shirt.

「夢中」 describes being absorbed in something and devoting one’s full attention to it. It fits the pattern 「〜に夢中で取り組む」, meaning to work on something with complete dedication.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q1.explanation: The noun/na-adjective 「夢中」(むちゅう) describes being absorbed in, engrossed in, or highly focused on something to the point of forgetting one’s surroundings. It commonly appears with に in 「〜に夢中になる」(be absorbed in something) or adverbially in 「〜に夢中で＋verb」(be completely absorbed in doing something). Therefore, (a) 「自分の仕事に夢中で取り組んでいる」is natural and means: “He is devoting all his attention and effort to his work.” Example: 「弟は時間を忘れて新しいゲームに夢中になっている。」(My younger brother is so absorbed in his new video game that he has forgotten the time.) Remember that 「夢中」refers to positive enthusiasm or concentration on an object. It is not used for physiological states such as deep sleep (which requires ぐっすり), sleepiness or absent-mindedness from lack of sleep (ぼんやり), or lowered vigilance after a victory (油断).
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q1.why.0: ✓ (a) The phrase「自分の仕事に夢中で取り組んでいる」is correct both grammatically and semantically for expressing wholehearted dedication to one's work.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) To describe sleeping so soundly that one cannot wake up until 9 a.m., use 「ぐっすり」or 「熟睡」, not 「夢中」.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) When lack of sleep while driving makes one's mind absent-minded or drowsy, the appropriate word is 「ぼんやり」 or 「うとうと」, not 「夢中」.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) After winning a match, the appropriate word for advising someone not to become careless or let their guard down is 「油断」. Using 「夢中」 in this context is completely incorrect.

Here, the noun 「声」 is used figuratively to mean opinions, views, or contributions, and combines naturally with 「耳をかたむける」(to listen carefully).
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q10.explanation: The noun 「声」(こえ) originally means the sound produced by a person’s or animal’s vocal organs, such as a voice or cry. In social contexts, it is often used figuratively to mean the "voice," opinions, or wishes of an individual or group. The complete sentence means: "You should open your mind and listen more carefully to other people’s voices and opinions." Compare: 「住民の声をしっかり聞いて、新しい計画を立てる。」 (Listen carefully to the residents’ voices before making a new plan.) At the N3 level, distinguish 「声」 (a sound produced by a living creature or an opinion) from 「音」 (a physical sound made by vehicles or objects), and do not confuse either with 「息」 (breath) or 「咳」 (a cough).
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q10.why.0: ✗ (a) Sounds produced by objects, machines, or vehicles require the noun 「音」(おと), not 「声」.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q10.why.1: ✗ (b) To describe running until one is exhausted and out of breath, the idiom 「息が切れる」(iki ga kireru) must be used instead of 「声」.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q10.why.2: ✗ (c) For the symptom of coughing continuously due to a cold, the noun「咳」(seki, a cough or coughing) must be used.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q10.why.3: ✓ (d) 「声」here expresses “other people’s voices or opinions,” forming a correct and natural expression.

✅ Correct answer: (b) 帰宅すると、家の前に（あやしい）男が立っていた。
The -i adjective「あやしい」(怪しい) means suspicious or dubious. It naturally modifies the noun「男」to describe a man behaving suspiciously.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q11.explanation: The -i adjective 「怪しい」 is used directly before a noun or as a predicate to express something suspicious, shady, unusual, or unsettling in a particular situation. The complete sentence can be understood as: “As soon as I arrived, I noticed a suspicious-looking man loitering right in front of my gate.” Another representative example is:「その男はあやしい笑みを浮かべてこちらを見ていた。」(That man looked at me with a sinister smile.) The key point is that 「怪しい」 is associated with negative or unclear things, so choices with positive, complimentary, or useful meanings, such as (a), (c), and (d), can be eliminated immediately.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q11.why.0: ✗ (a) The preceding clause says that it is cold, so a word such as 温かい (warm) is needed to describe the food; it cannot be combined with あやしい, meaning suspicious.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q11.why.1: ✓ (b) The phrase 「あやしい男」describes a man whose behavior is strange or suspicious, making it completely accurate and natural in this context.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q11.why.2: ✗ (c) The clause praises someone who is loved by everyone, so it must be followed by a positive adjective such as 優しい. A negative word such as あやしい cannot be used.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q11.why.3: ✗ (d) A notebook that can be used to write anything is a useful item, so it suits 便利 (“convenient” or “useful”), not あやしい.

✅ Correct answer: (c) 私の家の犬は、夜中によく（ほえます）。
The verb ほえる (吠える) means “to bark” or “to howl,” and is used to describe the natural sounds made by animals such as dogs or wild beasts.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q2.explanation: The Group 2 verb ほえる（吠える・吼える）is used to describe the loud, threatening, or warning sounds made by dogs (to bark) and wild animals (to growl or howl). Thus, the complete sentence in option (c) means: “The dog we keep at home often barks loudly in the middle of the night.” To avoid being misled by the other options, remember that ほえる is distinguished from 鳴く, used for birds, small animals, and insects, and 泣く, used when people shed tears from sadness or pain. Another useful example is: 「知らない人が近づくと、番犬が激しくほえた。」 (When a stranger approached, the guard dog barked fiercely.)
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q2.why.0: ✗ (a) In Japanese, the sound made by an insect (虫) is expressed with the verb 鳴く (なく), not ほえる.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q2.why.1: ✗ (b) When expressing casual conversation like friends (友だちのように) with a superior, use a verb such as 話す or しゃべる, not ほえる.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q2.why.2: ✓ (c) The verb ほえる (吠える) means “to bark” and combines exactly and naturally with a subject referring to a dog (犬).
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q2.why.3: ✗ (d) When a person feels sad and cries after their pet dies, the verb 泣く (なく) must be used, not ほえる.

The verb 「あふれる」means that a liquid rises beyond a container’s capacity and spills over, which fits the situation of pouring water into a cup.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q3.explanation: The intransitive verb「あふれる」(溢れる) fundamentally means to fill beyond a container's capacity and spill over. It is commonly used for liquids and, by extension, for crowds and surging emotions. In sentence (b), it accurately describes the situation: "As soon as I poured water into the glass, it overflowed." Distinguish「あふれる」(overflowing because something exceeds its capacity) from「こぼれる」(a liquid spilling because something is tilted or handled carelessly) and「余る」(being excessive in quantity). Another typical example is:「大雨のせいで川の水があふれた。」(Because of the heavy rain, the river overflowed its banks.)
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q3.why.0: ✗ (a) When sweets have been bought in excessive quantities and there is a surplus, use 「余る」(あまる), not「あふれる」.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q3.why.1: ✓ (b) 「あふれる」 accurately describes liquid being poured until it exceeds the cup's capacity and spills over.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q3.why.2: ✗ (c) To indicate that a student remains or is left in the classroom after class, the appropriate word is「残る」(のこる).
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q3.why.3: ✗ (d) To describe a leg becoming swollen and red after tripping on the street, the correct verb is 「腫れる」(はれる).

The verb「しばる」（縛る）means to tie, bind, or fasten something tightly with a rope or cord, so it fits naturally and accurately in the context of tying up a package.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t33-q4.explanation: The group 1 verb「しばる」（縛る）basically means to wrap a soft cord, rope, or twine around something and tie it tightly to secure it, as in「[object] を [means] でしばる」. The complete dialogue means: Customer: “What country is this clothing from?” — Staff member: “This outfit is from France.” Another familiar example is 「こちらは営業部でございます。」(This is the Sales Department.) Do not confuse 「でございます」, the noun equivalent of 「です」, with 「でおります」, the humble form of 「ています」, which is used for the speaker’s actions.

default.q.chokuzen_n3-t36-q10.why.1: ✗ (b) 「います」expresses the presence of a living being and does not form the combination 「〜でいます」with a noun to express an assertion.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t36-q10.why.2: ✗ (c) 「いらっしゃいます」 is respectful language used to elevate the other person’s action or existence. It cannot be used for an item being introduced.

The key to avoiding confusion with the respectful form in option (b) is to identify the subject: the person who heard the information and is asking about it is the speaker, so a respectful form must not be used for the speaker’s own action. The complete sentence means: “I heard that Mr. Tanaka lived in the United States when he was young. To advise or ask someone not to show fear, the emotional adjective 「こわい」 must be converted into a verb with the suffix 「〜がる」, becoming 「こわがる」, and then changed to the negative request form 「〜ないでください」.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q6.explanation: Emotion and psychological-state adjectives such as 「こわい」 (“scary” or “afraid”) are normally used for the speaker’s own feelings. To describe another person’s outwardly displayed attitude or reaction, use 「i-adjective (drop い) / na-adjective (drop な) / Vたい (drop い) + がる」 to form a group 1 verb. Therefore, to advise or ask the listener not to show fear, 「こわい」 must become 「こわがる」 and then be conjugated as 「こわがらないで（ください）」. The completed sentence means: “This dog may look fierce, but it is actually very gentle, so please don’t be afraid.” Choice (a) is tempting because of the literal translation “do not become afraid,” but remember that emotion adjectives must change through 「〜がる」 before combining with the advice/request patterns 「〜ないで／〜てください」, rather than with 「〜くなる」. A similar example is:「注射をそんなに怖がらないで、深呼吸してください。」(Please don’t be so afraid of the injection; take a deep breath.)
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q6.why.0: ✗ (a) An i-adjective describing a subjective emotional state cannot be used directly in the form「〜くならないで」to make a request or give advice to someone.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q6.why.1: ✗ (b) Incorrect because 「こわくしないで」 means to cause something to become frightening, which is completely unrelated to the context.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q6.why.2: ✗ (c) The progressive passive structure 「こわがられないでいて」is cumbersome, unnatural, and does not express the intended meaning.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q6.why.3: ✓ (d) This is correct because the pattern “i-adjective minus い + がる” changes an emotion into an outward behavior of another person, and combining it with 「〜ないで」forms an appropriate piece of advice.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q7.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) し
The conjunction particle 「し」follows the plain form to give one representative reason. When used with 「も」, it implies that there are additional reasons as well, supporting the refusal in the following clause.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q7.explanation: The pattern 「plain form (普通形) + し」 is widely used in everyday conversation to list reasons. When combined with 「も」 in 「～もあるし」, the speaker gives one representative reason while implying that other reasons also exist. The dialogue means: Matsuda: “Are you going out drinking today?” — Takenaka: “I also have to prepare for tomorrow’s test, so I am not going out today.” Another example is: 「疲れたし、明日も仕事があるから、もう帰ります。」 (“I am tired, and I have work tomorrow too, so I am going home now.”) Do not choose 「けど」 simply because of translation habits. 「けど」 expresses contrast, whereas here the second clause is a natural result of the reason about preparing for the test, so 「し」 correctly expresses the reason-and-result relationship.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q7.why.0: ✗ (a) 「けど」 expresses contrast or opposition (but/however), so it is unsuitable because not going out for drinks is a logical result of being busy studying for an exam.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q7.why.1: ✗ (b) 「と」is generally used to connect nouns or express a conditional “when/if...then” relationship; it is not used to explain the reason for a personal decision in this context.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q7.why.2: ✓ (c) 「し」 follows the plain form and combines with the particle 「も」 to give a representative reason for refusing the invitation.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q7.why.3: ✗ (d) 「まで」indicates a time or scope limit ("up to" or "until"), so it is unsuitable both grammatically and semantically in this position.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q8.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) あんな
The demonstrative 「あんな」directly modifies the following noun and refers to the negatively characterized subject just mentioned, clearly expressing the speaker’s dislike and exasperation.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q8.explanation: The structure 「あんな ＋ noun」modifies a noun and refers to an object the speaker is recalling or imagining with strong emotion, especially criticism, dissatisfaction, or contempt. The full sentence means: "The food was terrible and the staff’s service was awful, so I never want to set foot in a restaurant like that again." To remember this irritated, negative use, compare it with: 「あんな失礼な人とは二度と話したくない。」(I never want to talk to such a rude person again.) Remember that 「どんな / どの」are question words, while 「ある」means “a certain” neutrally and cannot express the speaker’s negative evaluation and avoidance as 「あんな」does.

default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q8.why.1: ✗ (b) 「どんな」 is an interrogative used to ask about qualities (“what kind of”), not in an affirmative sentence referring to a specific matter.

default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q8.why.3: ✗ (d) 「どの」 is an interrogative used to identify one item within a group (“which”); it is not used to describe a noun’s qualities in this context.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q9.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) ことから
This pattern expresses a reason, basis, or source leading to a conclusion or the origin of a name.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q9.explanation: The grammar pattern 〜ことから combines with the plain form of verbs, i-adjectives, na-adjectives with な or である, and nouns with である. It has a formal written style and expresses the basis for an inference or the origin of something. It often appears with naming patterns such as 「〜という名前が付いた」 (was given the name...) or 「〜と呼ばれる」 (is called...). The complete sentence means: “Because Mount Fuji can be seen clearly from this town, it was named Fujimi Town (Fujimi, literally “Fuji View”).” Compare: 「星がきれいに見えることから、この丘は『星見丘』と名付けられた。」 (Because the stars can be seen beautifully, this hill was named Hoshimi Hill.) Do not confuse it with 〜ことに, which expresses emotions such as 「うれしいことに」 (fortunately), or 〜ことだから, which makes an inference based on someone's usual character. Remember that 「から」 conveys the idea of an origin or source, making it easier to identify the basis or background of an event.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q9.why.0: ✗ (a) 「ことに」 is commonly used in the pattern 「〜ことに（は）」 to express the speaker’s emotion (“how...,” “to one’s...”), so it is unsuitable in a context indicating the basis or reason for naming something.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q9.why.1: ✓ (b) 「ことから」 is correct because it follows the plain form to state the basis or reason leading to a conclusion—in this case, the town being named Fujimi because Mount Fuji can be seen clearly.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q9.why.2: ✗ (c) 「ことを」 functions only as the object particle before a transitive verb; it does not form a linking structure expressing the cause or origin of something.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t41-q9.why.3: ✗ (d) 「ことは」 is mainly used to make a clause the topic or in the contrastive structure 「〜ことは〜が」; it does not indicate cause or origin.

✅ Correct answer: (c) 人生というものだ
The structure 「〜というものだ」is used to make a profound generalization, asserting that the preceding phenomenon represents the essential nature of life.

The complete sentence means: "I think that when something good happens after a series of hardships, that is what life is all about." A similar example is:「困ったときにお互いに助け合うのが、本当の友情というものだ」(Helping each other in difficult times—that is what true friendship is.) Do not confuse it with「〜というところだ」, which is mainly used to estimate an amount or degree ("it is only about..."). default.q.chokuzen_n3-t42-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) 「まま」expresses maintaining an unchanged state, so attaching it after 「という」to function as the predicate in this context is completely ungrammatical.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t42-q10.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) だったとしたら
The sentence expresses a counterfactual assumption about the present combined with 「～のに」, which conveys regret. Therefore, 「～としたら」is the only correct hypothetical form.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t42-q10.explanation: The structure「plain form + としたら」(with だ/だった after a noun) presents a hypothetical condition meaning “suppose” or “if.” It is especially common for imaginary situations that are unreal or unlikely at present. The complete sentence means: “If I were the prime minister of this country, I would have made its politics better, but...” implying regret because I am not actually the prime minister. Example:「もし生まれ変われるとしたら、鳥になりたい。」(If I could be reincarnated, I would want to become a bird.) Do not confuse it with「～にしたら」(from someone’s perspective or standpoint). default.q.chokuzen_n3-t42-q10.why.1: ✓ (b) The pattern「～としたら」introduces a hypothetical condition, meaning "if" or "suppose that..." It is entirely appropriate for the imaginary situation "if I were prime minister," followed by regret in the second clause.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t42-q10.why.2: ✗ (c) The pattern「～にしたら」means “from someone's standpoint” or “speaking as someone,” and is not used to set up a hypothetical condition.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t42-q10.why.3: ✗ (d) The pattern 「～にしては」expresses an evaluation contrary to the usual standard (“for...,” “considering...”); it does not fit the meaning here.

✅ Correct answer: (d) 遊びに行こうと
The verb 行く changes to the volitional form 行こう and combines with と思います to form「V-ようと思う」, expressing the speaker’s intention or desire to do something.

It differs from 「V-ようと思っている」, which usually describes a plan formed earlier. Since tomorrow is a rare day off after a busy period, the sentence 「明日、ひさしぶりの休みなので、町へ遊びに行こうと思います」 means: “Tomorrow is my first day off in a long time, so I intend to go into town for some fun.” Another example is: 「今週末は家でゆっくり好きな映画を見ようと思います」 (“This weekend, I intend to relax at home and watch a movie I like.”) Do not confuse it with the decision pattern 「〜ことにする」 in choice (a). That pattern takes 「する」 or 「した」, as in 遊びに行くことにしました, and never directly becomes 「ことに思う」. When 「思います」 follows, first look for the volitional form 「〜よう／おう」.

default.q.chokuzen_n3-t42-q11.why.1: ✗ (b) This is incorrect because there is no 「V-る + のにしようと思う」 pattern for expressing intention; this combination is grammatically invalid.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t42-q11.why.2: ✗ (c) Incorrect because 「〜ほどだ」 indicates degree (“to the extent that…”), which is completely unsuitable for expressing the intention in this sentence.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t42-q11.why.3: ✓ (d) The verb 「行く」 changes to the volitional form 「行こう」 and combines perfectly with 「思います」 in the pattern 「V-ようと思う」 to express the speaker’s intention to go into town.

The complete translation is: "Since there are neither buses nor trains running through this town, we have no choice but to walk." Another example is: 終電を逃してしまったので、タクシーで帰るよりほかはない。(I missed the last train, so I have no choice but to go home by taxi.) Since the basic meaning is “there is no other option besides this,” the expression must end in 「ない」, which lets you eliminate a and c. default.q.chokuzen_n3-t42-q13.why.1: ✓ (b) This is correct because the pattern「V-る + よりほか（は）ない」precisely expresses that there is no choice other than walking.

✅ Correct answer: (c) できないこともない
The preceding clause presents the condition 「がんばれば」 (“if one makes an effort”), so the following clause needs the potential form with double negation, 「できないこともない」, meaning “it is not necessarily impossible to do.”

They indicate that something is difficult but still possible under favorable conditions or with effort. The sentence means: “This job looks very demanding, but I think it’s not impossible if I try hard.” Another example: 「少し遠いですが、歩いて行けないこともないです。」 (It is a little far, but it is not impossible to walk there.) Do not confuse 「〜こともある」, which expresses occasional occurrence, with 「〜ないこともない」. default.q.chokuzen_n3-t42-q14.why.1: ✗ (b) This choice uses the wrong verb (なる) and is also grammatically incorrect because the pattern 〜ことがある (sometimes/occasionally) does not fit after the conditional effort clause がんばれば.

The complete sentence translates as: "I have a job interview tomorrow, so I absolutely must make sure I am not late." Learners may confuse this with choice (b) if they only notice 「ように」, but the ending 「〜と」 in (b) is merely a conditional conjunction that leaves the sentence incomplete, whereas the ending 「〜ないと」 in (d) expresses the obligation required by 「絶対に」. When referring to information just mentioned by the other speaker—in this case, the quantity of 50 copies—the demonstrative from the ソ series, 「それ」, is required.

When a speaker refers to information just mentioned by the other person in a conversation, the ソ-series must be used; here, 「それ」 refers to the quantity of 50 copies and combines with 「くらい」 to form 「それくらい」, meaning approximately that amount. A simple way to distinguish the ソ-series from the ア-series in conversation is this: if the information was just stated by one speaker, the other speaker uses the ソ-series (それ); the ア-series (あれ) is used when the information belongs to shared prior knowledge or experience. The complete dialogue is: Student: "Teacher, I have already printed 50 copies of the materials for the exchange event. Will that be enough?" — Teacher: "There are only 40 participants, so about that many will be fine." For comparison: 「１万円貸してくれませんか。」ー「それくらいなら、貸せますよ。」 ("Could you lend me 10,000 yen?" — "I can lend you about that much.").

In the question, using 「までに」creates the sentence: “I plan to finish writing this report by tomorrow evening.” Do not confuse it with 「まで」(until), which accompanies verbs expressing continuous actions. Remember that 「までに」combines with punctual or completed actions such as 「終える」,「提出する」, and 「帰る」. Example: 「明日の正午までにこの書類を提出してください。」(Please submit this document by noon tomorrow.)

default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q36.why.1: ✗ (b) 「までは」emphasizes the extent to which an action or continuous state lasts, and is not used to indicate the deadline for a definitive action.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q36.why.2: ✗ (c) The phrase 「までの」 modifies a noun that follows it, according to the structure N1 までの N2, whereas the word immediately following the blank is the verb 「書き終える」.

default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q37.explanation: The pattern 「Vて + ばかりいる」 (or noun + ばかり) is used when an action occurs continuously or repeatedly much more than normal, conveying the speaker's complaint, irritation, or criticism. The complete test sentence means: “The high school girl does nothing but fool around every day.” To distinguish it from 「しか」, which also means “only,” remember that 「しか」 must be followed by a negative ending (しか～ない), whereas 「ばかり」 combines with the affirmative 「～ている」 to emphasize excessive, objectionable repetition. For example: 「弟は勉強もしないで、ゲームをしてばかりいる。」(My younger brother does not study at all and does nothing but play video games.)
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q37.why.0: ✗ (a) 「より」 is a particle indicating comparison or a point of reference. It does not follow the て-form of a verb to create a suitable grammar pattern in this sentence.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q37.why.1: ✗ (b) 「しか」means “only” but must be used with a predicate in the negative form (しか～ない); it cannot be used with the affirmative 「いる」at the end.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q37.why.2: ✗ (c) 「から」 after a verb in the 「Vて」 form means “after doing something,” and it cannot directly combine with 「いる」 to create a meaningful sentence.

✅ Correct answer: (a) 一方で
The pattern 「〜一方で」describes two contrasting aspects of the same issue. It highlights the paradox that Japan must import much of its food while throwing away a great deal of food every day.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q38.explanation: The grammar pattern 「〜一方で（は）」combines directly with the plain form of a verb or adjective, or with a noun followed by である. It expresses two contrasting or simultaneously existing aspects of the same subject or situation. In the test context, the complete sentence means: "On the one hand, Japan imports most of its food, but on the other hand, a great deal of food is thrown away every day." Another example is: 「この仕事は給料が高い一方で、残業が多くて体力的にきつい。」(This job pays well, but on the other hand, it involves a lot of overtime and is physically demanding.) When two clauses present opposing or contrasting aspects, 「一方で」is a strong choice. Do not confuse it with 「だけで」, which expresses limitation, such as "only by" or "just by."
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q38.why.0: ✓ (a) This is correct because the pattern「V-plain form + 一方で」expresses two opposing or contrasting aspects of the same issue.

default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q38.why.3: ✗ (d) The pattern「〜だけなら」means “if it is only...” and does not fit the context of describing a present fact with an opposite outcome.

✅ Correct answer: (b) 悪くて
The i-adjective 「悪い」 changes to the te-form 「悪くて」 to express a cause leading to an objective result or a resulting inability, such as being unable to go out.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q39.explanation: In N3 grammar, the pattern「～て／～なくて」(with い-adjectives changing to「～くて」) is used when the preceding clause is a natural cause leading to an objective result beyond the speaker’s control, such as a physical condition or emotion. Therefore, the following clause cannot be an imperative or express volition. Since the following clause is「行けません」(the objective negative potential form),「悪くて」is the correct choice, producing the meaning: “I have not felt well since this morning, so I cannot go out today.” A similar example is:「頭が痛くて、勉強に集中できません。」(I have a headache, so I cannot concentrate on studying.) To avoid confusion with (d)「悪さで」, remember that「Noun + で」usually expresses a cause using nouns for illnesses or disasters, such as「病気で」or「風邪で」. It is not used here with the nominalized degree expression「～さ」to explain the speaker’s health condition.

default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q39.why.2: ✗ (c) 悪いことと combines the nominalizer こと with the particle と, but does not form a grammatical structure expressing a cause-and-effect relationship in Japanese.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q39.why.3: ✗ (d) 悪さで is a nominalized form referring to the degree of badness or mischievous behavior, used with the particle で; it is not a natural way to express the reason for poor health.

✅ Correct answer: (c) 見るほど
This sentence uses the correlative pattern 「V-れば V-るほど」 (“the more ..., the more ...”). The element before 「ほど」 must be the dictionary form of the same verb used in the 「ば」 clause.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q40.explanation: The grammar pattern 「V-れば V-るほど」 expresses a proportional relationship meaning “the more..., the more...”. It is used when an increasing degree or frequency of an action causes a corresponding change in the following state. In the standard pattern, the first verb is changed to the conditional 「～ば」 form, while the word immediately before 「ほど」 must be the dictionary form of that same verb. Thus, 「この子ねこは、見れば見るほどかわいい。」means: “The more you look at this kitten, the cuter it seems.” Compare it with: 「日本語は勉強すればするほど面白くなります。」(“The more you study Japanese, the more interesting it becomes.”) A quick test-taking tip is to identify the verb in the 「ば」 clause and choose its dictionary form before 「ほど」. Do not choose forms such as the volitional form (見よう), negative form (見ない), or past form (見た).
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q40.why.0: ✗ (a) 見よう is the volitional form, and this grammar pattern does not allow a volitional form before「ほど」.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q40.why.1: ✗ (b) 見ない is the negative form and does not follow the rule for repeating a verb to express an increasing degree.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q40.why.2: ✓ (c) 見る is the dictionary form of the verb 見る and correctly combines with the preceding clause to form the grammatical structure 「見れば見るほど」.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q40.why.3: ✗ (d) 見た is the ta-form (past form), and the grammar rules do not allow a past form before 「ほど」.

Learners often confuse it with the te-form because of request patterns, or with the dictionary form. However, when giving direct personal advice, the verb should generally be conjugated into the past た-form. Applied to the question,「来年の試験を受けるなら、今から勉強を始めたほうがいい。」means: "If you plan to take next year’s exam, you should start studying now." default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q41.why.1: ✓ (b) This is correct because the past た-form verb (始めた) combines with ほうがいい to form the pattern 〜たほうがいい, used to give advice about what someone should do.

It is used when there is too much of something or the degree is too great for the subject to deal with it completely. The complete sentence means: "There is so much food at this restaurant that I can't possibly finish it all." Another typical example is:「数えきれないほどの星が夜空に輝いている。」(Countless stars are shining in the night sky.) As a test-taking tip, when a grammar pattern expressing excess such as「〜すぎて」(too much...) appears before it, the following clause must express a limit of ability using the negative potential form「〜きれない」, rather than an ordinary negative action form such as (a) or (b).
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q42.why.0: ✗ (a) “食べきってない” indicates that the act of eating has not been completed at the time of speaking; it does not express being unable to eat everything.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q42.why.1: ✗ (b) “食べきらない” is simply a negative form expressing intention or habit. It cannot convey the inability to finish because the amount of food is too large.

default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q42.why.3: ✗ (d) The combination「食べきりがない」does not exist in Japanese grammar.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q43.verdict:

Because the subject is 先生 (teacher, a superior), the honorific form「お＋V(ます-stem)＋になる」must be used to show respect for the action of returning.
default.q.chokuzen_n3-t76-q43.explanation: In Japanese honorific language,「お＋V(stem)＋になる」is used with group 1 and group 2 verbs in the continuative form. It commonly takes the particle に to state the cause, as in「お金に困る」, or appears in the pattern「〜て困る」when complaining. The complete sentence「生活で困ることは何ですか。」means: "What things cause you difficulty in daily life?" Another example: 「財布を落としてしまって、本当に困りました。」(I lost my wallet and was truly in trouble.) A common conversational example is 「どんなときも家族は私の味方でいてくれる」 (“My family always stands by me, no matter what.”) At N3 level, use the kanji to distinguish the homophones: 「見方」, with 見, means “viewpoint” or “perspective,” while 「味方」, with 味 and 方, means “ally” or “someone on one’s side.”

default.p.chokuzen_n3-t58-p1.vietnamese:
Paper Planners

Ever since personal computers and mobile phones became widely used, an increasing number of people have been using them instead of planners to manage their personal schedules. Even so, aren't there still many people who want to buy paper planners? I am one of them as well.

At the planner section of a certain bookstore, they began selling planners for the upcoming year around the end of summer. Previously, speaking of planners, simple ones with black covers were the most common; however, when I asked the store clerk, I learned that products specifically targeted at young women have recently been on the rise. Although planners for women have been sold for some time, this year there seems to be a particularly wide variety. For example, items that young women are likely to favor are fully stocked: planners in bright, lovely colors such as pink, ones featuring cute designs, types that allow you to attach your favorite pen, and ones equipped with fastening bands or ribbons to keep them closed. Since I also use a planner frequently for work, having more options to enjoy choosing from makes me very happy.

However, even when I tried to pick one out at the sales counter, there were so many different items that I could not decide immediately. I think I will first think over what kind of planner I truly want before heading to the store.

default.p.chokuzen_n3-t59-p1.outline.0.label: Childhood expectations

default.p.chokuzen_n3-t59-p1.outline.1.label: Reality challenges expectations

default.p.chokuzen_n3-t59-p1.outline.4.label: From self-doubt to empathy
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t59-p1.outline.4.note: The narrator wonders whether they have become worse than in childhood, then feels warmth at the thought that their parents may also have struggled to grow into adulthood.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t59-p1.vietnamese:
When I Become an Adult

As a child, I thought that when I reached my parents’ age, I would surely become a more admirable person. For example, I still want to keep sleeping in the morning, just as I did as a child. Moreover, when work is tough, I often find myself wanting to take time off. Yet, when I actually reach the age at which I once thought I would be an “adult,” I am surprised to find that I have not matured. I have even gone so far as to lie, saying, “I have a fever from a cold,” and actually take time off work. And yet, as a child, I used to attend school faithfully even when I really had a fever.

Also, I still dislike foods I hated as a child, such as carrots and green peppers, so I make a point of avoiding them when they are in a dish. Despite that, I sometimes scold my own children self-importantly, saying, “Don’t be picky. Eat everything!”

Now that I have become an adult who shirks responsibilities and can lie skillfully like that, perhaps, far from having matured, I have become worse inside than I was as a child. And when I think that my parents, whom I regarded as “adults” long ago, may also have thought as I do now and struggled to become “adults,” I feel a certain warmth inside.

default.p.chokuzen_n3-t60-p1.vietnamese:
New city emblem unveiled

Mayor Aoki of City A unveiled a new city emblem featuring a tulip motif. According to the Public Relations Section at City A's city hall, the new emblem is said to convey a message from Mayor Aoki. The design is said to feature a tulip, City A's official flower, at its center, with small surrounding patterns depicting residents living happily. The ward head proposed the initial idea for this emblem, wanting it to evoke a sense of approachability and warmth, and had a designer living in City A create it.

Starting today, City A will make the new emblem publicly available on its website. The city also plans to create a mascot based on this emblem soon and invite name suggestions from residents at large.

In Japan, cities, towns, and villages have various mascots that have become popular figures. Very popular mascots sometimes appear on merchandise such as handkerchiefs or are featured on television. The mayor says he wants residents to think of a name that many people will love and give it to City A's mascot as well.

default.p.chokuzen_n3-t62-p1.vietnamese:
How to store newspapers

To obtain a variety of information, I make a point of reading not only Japanese-language newspapers but English-language newspapers as well. This is a habit I have maintained for ten years. Through this, I not only obtain information but also learn English. Thanks to having read for a long time, I can now grasp the general content just by skimming from the first page onward.

However, there is one problem. It is how to organize and store the growing collection of newspapers so that they are easy to find. Since I buy English-language newspapers every week, if I simply stack them up and leave them as they are, I will lose track of where an old newspaper is when I want to read it again. For someone like me who loves reading newspapers, throwing away old newspapers is unthinkable.

So I tried various approaches and recently finally found a way to solve this problem. The method is to sort the newspapers by year and month, put them in boxes, and keep them stored there. Although it is a simple method, it has turned out to be the most efficient way to store newspapers, and I can now retrieve them immediately. There is an exciting kind of pleasure in looking through old newspapers.
