default.p.chokuzen_n3-t63-p1.sentences.16.keys.0: The expression '～ということでしょうか' means 'could it mean that...? / is it that...?', expressing gentle rhetorical reflection derived from the fact that the author has gotten used to hot bathwater like a Japanese person. Options 1 (限り), 2 (どころ), and 3 (上) do not form an appropriate reflective question in this context.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t63-p1.outline.0.label: Introduction: The Sento (Public Bath)
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t63-p1.outline.0.note: Author Pierre Martin introduces Japanese bath culture and states that in his personal case, sento (public bathhouse) is what comes to mind.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t63-p1.outline.1.label: Surprise at the Japanese Daily Bathing Custom
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t63-p1.outline.1.note: The author contrasts Japan with his hometown to highlight his surprise at the Japanese daily bathing habit (at home or at a sento), a custom rare in the world.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t63-p1.outline.2.label: Four Surprises on the First Visit to a Sento
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t63-p1.outline.2.note: The author lists in sequence four surprising aspects from his first sento visit: temple-like architecture, separate male/female entrances, nakedness in public, and extremely hot water.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t63-p1.outline.3.label: Gradual Adaptation and Feeling More Japanese
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t63-p1.outline.3.note: The author notes that he is growing accustomed to sento, enjoying the hot water comfortably, and wonders if he has come closer to living like a Japanese person.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t63-p1.vietnamese:
My First Time at a Public Bath
Pierre Martin

When you think of Japanese baths, what comes to mind? Could it be a hot spring, or perhaps an open-air bath? There are various kinds, but in my case, it is the "sento" (public bathhouse).
In my hometown, there is no custom of taking a bath every day. Therefore, when I had just arrived in Japan, I was very surprised to learn that Japanese people bathe daily. Those who have a bathtub at home take a bath at home every day, and even those who do not go to the neighborhood sento almost every day. I think there are very few ethnic groups in the wide world that have this kind of custom.
When I visited a sento for the first time, there were many things that surprised me. First of all, the building was a very old structure that looked like a Buddhist temple or a Shinto shrine. Second, the entrance was separated into a "men's bath" and a "women's bath." Third, I had to take off all my clothes in front of other people before entering the bath. Finally, the temperature of the bathwater was extremely hot.
However, nowadays I am gradually getting used to Japanese public baths as well. I have become able to relax and soak comfortably in hot water without minding anything. Could it mean that I, too, have grown quite close to becoming "Japanese"?
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.0.vi: A new name is chosen for the shopping street
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.0.grammar: Indicates that something is decided; 決まる is intransitive.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.1.vi: A shopping street invited suggestions for a new name.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.1.grammar: Invite applications or submissions; here, suggestions for a name.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.2.vi: As a result, there were as many as approximately 1,000 submissions.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.2.grammar: After a quantity, も emphasizes how large it is, and の links it to a noun: 約１０００通もの応募. Choose option 2.
Expresses that something existed or occurred.
The large quantity is emphasized with もの: as many as approximately 1,000 submissions.
The noun 応募 takes の after the emphasized quantity; affirmative あった also rules out しか.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.3.vi: The shop owners discussed the suggestions and chose the best one, deciding on a new name for the shopping street.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.3.grammar: Select from a group or set; その中 refers to the submitted names.
Links actions in sequence: discussing, choosing, and reaching a result.
Stands for a noun understood from context, here a suggested name; unlike the quantity-emphasizing もの in the previous sentence.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.4.grammar: Introduces a name: be called or be named.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.5.vi: Until now, it had been called “Furukawa Street” after an old place name in the town, so the new name may come as a surprise to people who have lived here for a long time.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.5.grammar: The passive combined with ～ていた describes a name used previously.
Gives a reason: the street previously had a name based on an old place name.
Marks the perspective or experience of a person or group.
Modifies a noun: 驚くような名前 is a name that could surprise people.
Expresses an uncertain possibility, often paired with もしかすると. It follows a noun directly without だ. Choose the pair in option 2.
The former name provides a basis for guessing reactions to the new name, rather than setting a hypothetical condition with もし or もしも.
The writer speculates about longtime residents’ feelings, matching もしかすると…かもしれない.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.6.vi: Aiming for a bright, lively name that would attract young people too, they chose the new name based on kiwi fruit, a local specialty.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.6.vocab.6: let us make; intend to choose
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.6.grammar: Marks inclusion: young people would come too.
Describes the desired character of the name: one that would attract young people.
The volitional form plus と expresses an intention or aim; here, 'intending to choose something…'.
A written equivalent of だ, used here in a modifier: fruit that is a local specialty.
Describes something created or decided based on a particular source.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.7.vi: This shopping street is an old street said to have existed for more than a hundred years or so.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.7.grammar: Emphasizes a long span extending from the past: since over… ago.
Embeds reported information in a noun modifier: a street said to have existed for a long time.
Introduces the street’s long history before 実は reveals its current problems in the next sentence.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.8.vi: In fact, the buildings and roads had recently been deteriorating, and various problems had begun to arise, including young motorcyclists gathering and making noise at night and crimes occurring.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.8.grammar: Expresses a gradual change up to the reference point: becoming older or more run-down.
Lists representative examples before summarizing them: noise, crimes, and other problems.
Describes a change that had taken place: problems had begun to occur.
Begins revealing the street’s recent condition; 実は appropriately introduces this background.
These problems explain the motive for renaming; the passage presents neither alternatives nor a concessive argument. Choose option 2: 実は.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.9.vi: In addition, a large shopping center opened nearby, and customer numbers also fell.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.9.grammar: でき is the connective stem of できる, here referring to a new facility being built or opening.
Adds another problem: customer numbers fell too.
Describes a completed outcome with regret or a sense that it was undesirable.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.10.vi: The people of the shopping street reportedly changed its name as one of their strategies to make the street as lively as it used to be.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.10.gramma: Nominalizes an action as the topic: changing the name is a strategy.
変える is transitive: someone changes something; 変わる is intransitive: something changes. 人たちが fits 名前を変えた.
Expresses similarity: as in the past.
States the strategy’s purpose: to make the street lively.
Reports information: reportedly; it is said that….
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.10.keys.0: The subject is the people carrying out the action, so use transitive 名前を変えた: changed the name. Choose option 1.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.10.keys.1: Renaming is a deliberate strategy to restore liveliness, rather than keeping the existing name.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.10.keys.2: The goal of reviving the street supports the following inference that shopkeepers eagerly hope to see results soon.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.11.vi: The shopkeepers must be hoping that the new name will produce results as soon as possible.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.11.gramma: Hope or pray for something to happen; こと nominalizes the clause about the name producing results soon.
Expresses a confident inference about someone’s current state: must be…. Choose option 1: 祈っているにちがいない.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.11.keys.0: The writer infers the shopkeepers’ feelings, fitting 祈っているにちがいない.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.sentences.11.keys.1: The hoped-for outcome is that the name produces results soon; this clause serves as the object of 祈る.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.outline.0.label: Choosing the new name
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.outline.0.note: The shopping street invites suggestions, receives approximately 1,000 submissions, and its shop owners choose “Kiwi Street.”
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.outline.1.label: The idea behind the name
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.outline.1.note: The name may surprise longtime residents; it draws on the local kiwi specialty and aims for a cheerful image that attracts young people.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.outline.2.label: The street’s current problems
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.outline.2.note: The old street faces deterioration, noise, crime, and falling customer numbers after a large shopping center opens nearby.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.outline.3.label: Renaming to restore liveliness
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.outline.3.note: Renaming is a strategy to restore the street’s former liveliness; the writer confidently infers that shopkeepers hope for quick results.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t64-p1.vietnamese:
A new name is chosen for the shopping street

A shopping street invited suggestions for a new name. As a result, there were as many as approximately 1,000 submissions. The shop owners discussed the suggestions and chose the best one, deciding on a new name for the shopping street. The new name is “Kiwi Street.”

Until now, it had been called “Furukawa Street” after an old place name in the town, so the new name may come as a surprise to people who have lived here for a long time. Aiming for a bright, lively name that would attract young people too, they chose the new name based on kiwi fruit, a local specialty.

This shopping street is an old street said to have existed for more than a hundred years or so. In fact, the buildings and roads had recently been deteriorating, and various problems had begun to arise, including young motorcyclists gathering and making noise at night and crimes occurring. In addition, a large shopping center opened nearby, and customer numbers also fell.

The people of the shopping street reportedly changed its name as one of their strategies to make the street as lively as it used to be. The shopkeepers must be hoping that the new name will produce results as soon as possible.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.0.grammar: Modifies a noun to indicate its intended beneficiaries: a seminar for working women.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.1.vi: This coming Sunday, the first session of “Job Seminar: New Ways of Living for Working Women,” a seminar program supporting working women, is scheduled to take place at the civic hall in front of the station.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.1.vocab.1: area in front of the station
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.1.grammar: A dictionary-form verb followed by ための expresses the purpose of the following noun: a seminar intended to support women.
Expresses a plan or scheduled event; 行われる予定です means “is scheduled to be held.”
行われる is the passive form of 行う; the session is the event being held.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.2.vi: Working women today have various roles, such as company employee, mother, wife, and daughter, and more and more of them are busy.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.2.grammar: States what someone or something has: working women have multiple roles.
Marks examples in a non-exhaustive list.
In 増えています, indicates an ongoing trend: the number of busy people is increasing.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.3.vi: However, despite becoming busier than before, the reality is that they have no one to help them.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.3.grammar: Marks the comparison baseline: 以前より means “than before.”
An い-adjective changes to its ～く form before なる to express a change of state.
The pattern required in blank 1-a means “despite” and introduces an outcome contrary to what the preceding situation might lead one to expect.
Indicates that someone performs an action benefiting the speaker or the person whose perspective is adopted.
The completed pattern after filling blank 1-b nominalizes the situation with の and identifies it as the current reality.
Being busier than before creates an expectation of support; にもかかわらず in 1-a connects this with the lack of help.
This describes an existing situation, so 1-b takes 現状です. The correct pair for question 1 is option 4.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.4.vi: In this seminar program, planned to comprise five sessions, women active in various industries will serve as speakers and explore future ways of living and effective ways of working for women together with the participants.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.4.grammar: されている in 活躍されている expresses respect for the female speakers' activities; it is not passive here.
A formal connective form of ～となる, indicating becoming or serving as a speaker.
Means “together with”; the speakers and participants will think together.
Expresses an activity continuing or developing into the future, here the ongoing exploration during the program.
Attaches to a verb stem to express how something is done: 生き方 means a way of living and 働き方 a way of working.
The discussion concerns women's ways of living and working going forward, so これからの is the appropriate modifier. Question 2 takes option 1.
The forward-looking process supports the future meaning of これからの; no past reference point is given for あれからの.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.5.vi: We are seeking participants who can not only listen to the talks but also ask questions and express their opinions.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.5.grammar: The required pattern means “not only ... but also ...,” adding active participation to listening.
Lists a representative action. Here 質問をしたり gives asking questions as an example; the original does not use the full paired ～たり…～たりする pattern.
言える is the potential form of 言う, meaning “can say” or “can express.”
方, read かた, is a polite word for a person; the preceding clause describes the participants being sought.
ただ emphasizes merely listening; the next clause adds active participation, requiring だけでなく.
Asking questions and expressing opinions are additional actions, not conditions. Question 3 takes option 3.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.6.vi: The speaker for the first session is Ms. Hanako Morikawa, who runs a company.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.6.grammar: The clause 会社を経営する directly modifies the person's name, explaining that Ms. Morikawa runs a company.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.7.vi: The seminar will be held on the theme “How Working Women Use Their Time.”
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.7.grammar: Indicates taking something as the theme of an activity.
The verb stem 使い plus 方 forms 使い方, meaning “how to use.”
仕事を持つ modifies 女性: women who have jobs.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.8.vi: After the talk, there will also be a party where the speaker and participants can socialize.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.8.grammar: Indicates a time after an event: after the talk.
A dictionary-form verb plus ことができる expresses ability or an opportunity to perform an action.
Adds another activity to those already introduced: there will also be a party.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.9.vi: Other details, such as the planned speaker schedule from the second session onward, are published on the civic hall's website.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.9.grammar: The required pattern means “from ... onward,” including the stated starting point. 第２回目以降 includes the second session and all subsequent sessions.
Shows that the speaker schedule is one example of the information published.
Introduces the topic being discussed: regarding the other details.
公開しています indicates that the information is currently published and available on the website.
This is a starting point in a sequence of sessions; 以降の means “from the second session onward,” including that session. Question 4 takes option 4.
The sentence directs readers to details of subsequent sessions, requiring a time-sequence expression rather than a quantity threshold or direction.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.10.vi: If you wish to participate, please register by calling the civic hall office directly.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.10.gramma: A polite expression referring to people who wish for something, here those who wish to participate.
Marks the destination for contact or registration: the civic hall office.
電話で specifies the means of contact: by telephone.
A polite request pattern; お申し込みください means “please register.”
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.11.vi: We look forward to your participation.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.11.gramma: The completed pattern politely means “we look forward to ...”. お待ちいたす is a humble form of 待つ, and ～ております is a humble, formal counterpart of ～ています.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.sentences.11.keys.0: The organizers are awaiting the readers' participation, so they use humble language for their own action: お待ちいたしております. Question 5 takes option 3.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.outline.0.label: Introducing the seminar
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces the intended audience, program title, and the time and location of the first session.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.outline.1.label: Working women's current situation
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.outline.1.note: Women have multiple roles and are increasingly busy, yet they have no one to help. This contrast leads to the pair にもかかわらず／現状です.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.outline.2.label: Goals and participation
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.outline.2.note: The five-session program explores women's future ways of living and working; participants should actively ask questions and express opinions as well as listen.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.outline.3.label: The first session
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.outline.3.note: Introduces speaker Hanako Morikawa, the theme of time use, and the social gathering after the talk.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.outline.4.label: Further information and registration
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.outline.4.note: Information from the second session onward is available online; interested participants register directly by phone. The notice ends with a formal expression of welcome.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t65-p1.vietnamese:
A Seminar for Working Women

This coming Sunday, the first session of “Job Seminar: New Ways of Living for Working Women,” a seminar program supporting working women, is scheduled to take place at the civic hall in front of the station.

Working women today have various roles, such as company employee, mother, wife, and daughter, and more and more of them are busy. However, despite becoming busier than before, the reality is that they have no one to help them.

In this seminar program, planned to comprise five sessions, women active in various industries will serve as speakers and explore future ways of living and effective ways of working for women together with the participants. We are seeking participants who can not only listen to the talks but also ask questions and express their opinions.

The speaker for the first session is Ms. Hanako Morikawa, who runs a company. The seminar will be held on the theme “How Working Women Use Their Time.” After the talk, there will also be a party where the speaker and participants can socialize.

Other details, such as the planned speaker schedule from the second session onward, are published on the civic hall's website. If you wish to participate, please register by calling the civic hall office directly. We look forward to your participation.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.0.grammar: Refers to matters concerning something; here it means “about…”.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.1.vocab.0: Zhang Tuo (author; reading given in Sino-Japanese)
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.2.vi: On Saturday and Sunday, I visited Mount Fuji for the first time since coming to Japan.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.2.grammar: Here, 日本に来て初めて means doing something for the first time since coming to Japan.
The polite past form recounts a completed trip.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.3.vi: Before I came to Japan, Mount Fuji was what represented Japan in my mind.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.3.grammar: A dictionary-form verb + 前 means “before doing”; は marks that time as the topic.
The clause 日本のイメージを代表する modifies もの: the thing representing the image of Japan.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.4.vi: When I thought about being able to climb Mount Fuji, I was so excited the night before that I could not sleep well.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.4.grammar: In the answer 登れると思うと, this means “when I think about…,” introducing the emotion that thought produces.
Potential forms express ability or opportunity: 登れる means “can climb,” and 眠れる means “can sleep.” 眠れませんでした is polite past negative.
The て-form of an い-adjective links an emotion to its result: being excited led to not sleeping well.
This is the night before the climb, so climbing is still ahead. 登れる fits, whereas past 登れた does not.
This describes excitement at the thought of the upcoming climb; question 1 takes option 1, 登れると思うと.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.5.vi: The tour I joined with my friend involved leaving early in the morning by bus, first riding to the fifth station, then following the guide up to the eighth station, staying overnight in a mountain hut, and heading for the summit the next morning.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.5.grammar: 私が友だちと一緒に参加した modifies ツアー, identifying the tour the author joined.
Means “following/in accordance with…”; here it refers to following the guide.
These continuative verb forms list actions in sequence. The し in 出発し is a form of する, not the reason-listing particle ～し.
Links successive actions, such as following the guide, climbing, staying overnight, and continuing to the summit.
Explains the content or nature of something just mentioned; here it outlines the tour itinerary.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.6.vi: Because the weather was very good, I was able to see the sunrise known as “goraiko” from the summit.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.6.vocab.4: sunrise viewed from a high mountain
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.6.grammar: Gives a cause: the good weather made it possible to see the sunrise.
Means “a noun called…”; ご来光 names the sunrise viewed from a high mountain.
In the answer, a dictionary-form verb + ことができました expresses something the speaker was able to do in the past.
The good weather enabled the author to actually see the sunrise; question 2 takes option 3, 見ることができました.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.7.grammar: The polite past form after a な-adjective describes an impression of something already seen.
The evaluation of the view supports an actual viewing experience, matching 見ることができました in question 2.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.8.vi: However, what disappointed me was that a lot of rubbish had been left there.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.8.vocab.4: had been discarded and left there
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.8.grammar: Nominalizes clauses in the pattern “what… is that…,” specifying what disappointed the author.
Passive + ていた describes a past resulting state: rubbish had been discarded and remained there.
Seeing much discarded rubbish prompts the decision in the next sentence, supporting そこで in question 3. It also supports よごれている in question 4.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.9.vi: So I decided to pick up rubbish with my friend on the way down.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.9.grammar: Specifies when an action takes place: picking up rubbish while descending.
A dictionary-form verb + ことにしました expresses a decision made by the subject.
そこで in the answer connects a situation to an action taken in response: seeing rubbish led to deciding to pick it up.
This is a decision responding to the rubbish just mentioned. Question 3 takes option 2, そこで, rather than a topic change or an unexpected contrast.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.10.vi: As I kept putting the rubbish I found into the bag I had brought, the rubbish bag was full by the time I returned to the fifth station.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.10.gramma: もっていた and 見つけた modify 袋 and ごみ respectively: the bag being carried and the rubbish found.
Expresses an action continuing as events progress: repeatedly putting rubbish into the bag during the descent.
Connects an action with an observed result: continuing to put rubbish in resulted in a full bag.
Means “by around the time…,” emphasizing a state already reached at that point.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.10.keys.0: Collecting a full bag demonstrates the amount of litter, reinforcing よごれている for blank 4-b.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.11.vi: I felt sad when I realized that Mount Fuji, which looks so beautiful from a distance, was actually this dirty.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.11.gramma: In 遠くから見ると, と sets a condition or perspective: “when viewed from a distance…”.
A な-adjective takes な before a noun: the answer きれいな modifies 富士山.
Contrasts appearance with reality: even Mount Fuji, despite looking so beautiful, has a contrasting actual condition.
Nominalizes a fact with こと and expresses realizing or discovering it.
Expresses a change in emotion: 悲しい気持ちになる means “feel sad.”
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.11.keys.0: Introduces the distant view; blank 4-a requires きれいな to describe 富士山.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.sentences.11.keys.1: Shifts to the actual littered condition described earlier; blank 4-b requires よごれている.

default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.outline.0.label: First visit and anticipation
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.outline.0.note: Introduces the title, author, and first visit to Mount Fuji since arriving in Japan. The mountain's symbolic image makes the author too excited to sleep well the night before.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.outline.1.label: The climb and sunrise
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.outline.1.note: Describes the route through the fifth and eighth stations, an overnight stay, and the ascent to the summit the next morning. Good weather allows the author to see and appreciate the sunrise.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.outline.2.label: Disappointment and collecting rubbish
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.outline.2.note: Joy turns to disappointment when the author sees much litter. This prompts the author and a friend to collect rubbish on the descent, filling a bag by the fifth station.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.outline.3.label: Distant beauty and actual conditions
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.outline.3.note: The author feels sad about the contrast between Mount Fuji's beauty from a distance and its actual littered condition. The guide also confirms that rubbish is a problem.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.outline.4.label: Research and a wish to help
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.outline.4.note: After returning, the author researches tours and learns about ones combining climbing with rubbish collection. The author wants to join one next time to help clean Mount Fuji.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t68-p1.vietnamese:
About Mount Fuji
Zhang Tuo

On Saturday and Sunday, I visited Mount Fuji for the first time since coming to Japan. Before I came to Japan, Mount Fuji was what represented Japan in my mind. When I thought about being able to climb it, I was so excited the night before that I could not sleep well.

The tour I joined with my friend involved leaving early in the morning by bus, first riding to the fifth station, then following the guide up to the eighth station, staying overnight in a mountain hut, and heading for the summit the next morning. Because the weather was very good, I was able to see the sunrise known as “goraiko” from the summit. It was truly beautiful.

However, what disappointed me was that a lot of rubbish had been left there. So I decided to pick up rubbish with my friend on the way down. As I kept putting the rubbish I found into the bag I had brought, the rubbish bag was full by the time I returned to the fifth station. I felt sad when I realized that Mount Fuji, which looks so beautiful from a distance, was actually this dirty. The guide also said that rubbish on Mount Fuji had become a problem.

After returning, I looked it up on my computer and found that there also seem to be tours where people pick up rubbish while climbing. To help make Mount Fuji clean, I thought I would like to join a tour like that next time.

default.p.chokuzen_n3-t69-p1.sentences.10.keys.2: Despite the room's condition, the inclination to tidy does not arise; this attitude also supports 思わない in question 5.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t69-p1.sentences.11.vi: The reasons are probably that a very neat room with everything organized actually makes me feel unsettled, and that I cannot set aside enough time to tidy up.

Nominalizes two clauses with こと and joins them with と to present two reasons.
Expresses being unable to secure or set aside something; 時間がとれない means being unable to make time.
Expresses probability; the author tentatively explains their own attitude.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t69-p1.sentences.11.keys.0: An overly neat room makes the author feel unsettled, explaining the lack of inclination in question 4 and supporting the negative conclusion in question 5.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t69-p1.sentences.11.keys.1: Lack of time is the second reason for not making a special effort to tidy, reinforcing option 4 in both questions 4 and 5.

default.p.chokuzen_n3-t69-p1.sentences.12.keys.0: Limits the conclusion to the present, without claiming the author will never tidy the room.

default.p.chokuzen_n3-t69-p1.outline.0.label: Many books about tidying
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t69-p1.outline.0.note: The title asks whether tidying is necessary. The opening introduces books on the topic and their authors; the question addressed to readers and the bookstore situation provide evidence for questions 1 and 2.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t69-p1.outline.1.label: From strong sales to widespread need
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t69-p1.outline.1.note: The author infers from strong book sales that many people struggle with tidying. This summarizing inference calls for 要するに.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t69-p1.outline.2.label: The author also lives with clutter
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t69-p1.outline.2.note: The author admits to being unable to tidy and describes a cluttered room and drawers. This is the situation referred to by そうであっても.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t69-p1.outline.3.label: Messy, yet disinclined to tidy
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t69-p1.outline.3.note: しかし introduces an unexpected attitude: the author does not feel like making a special effort to tidy. The two reasons are feeling unsettled in a very neat room and being unable to make enough time.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t69-p1.outline.4.label: No current intention to read books to tidy
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t69-p1.outline.4.note: The author concludes that, for now, they do not intend to go as far as reading instructional books to tidy their room. This is a personal conclusion, not a claim that nobody needs to tidy.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t69-p1.vietnamese:
Is tidying up necessary?

Did you know that many books have been published on the themes of cleaning, tidying up, and organizing? “How to Become a Cleaning Expert,” “You Too Can Become Someone Who Can Tidy Up!”, “The Art of Organizing Your Room”... When you visit a bookstore, it is not as though you never come across books with titles like these. The authors are sometimes celebrities and sometimes ordinary people. Either way, there is no doubt that the books were written by “tidying experts.”

Moreover, books of this kind seem to be selling well. In short, this probably means that there are correspondingly many people in the world who cannot tidy up or are poor at organizing.

In fact, I too am one of those people who cannot tidy up. My room is always dirty and messy. The desk drawers are packed with things, and books, clothes, and all sorts of other items are piled up around the room.

However, speaking for myself, even so, I do not feel inclined to go out of my way to organize and tidy up my surroundings. The reasons are probably that a very neat room with everything organized actually makes me feel unsettled, and that I cannot set aside enough time to tidy up.

For now, I have no intention of going so far as to read books on organizing and tidying in order to tidy my room.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.0.grammar: Rhetorical question / self-questioning expression wondering whether something is truly the case.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.1.vi: In Japan, people are often made to hear that English education is very important.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.1.grammar: The talk/story that... (used to define the content of what is spoken).
Passive-causative form of 聞く: to be made to listen to / repeatedly told something by others.
The phrase '話を聞かされる' uses the causative-passive form of the verb 聞く to express being repeatedly subjected to hearing something from people around oneself, perfectly matching the context where people in Japan are constantly told that English education is important. Option 1 (よく聞かれる) means being asked or serves as honorific, Option 2 (よく聞かせる) means telling someone else, and Option 4 (よく聞くようにさせる) means making someone listen, none of which fit the meaning and sentence structure.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.2.vi: First of all, in schools, there are hours dedicated to studying English from elementary school through high school.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.2.grammar: From... to... (indicating a continuous span of time or stages).
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.3.vi: Furthermore, even after joining the workforce, there are very many people who attend English conversation schools or take various certification exams, either voluntarily or at their company's instruction.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.3.grammar: Even after entering a new stage in life (here, after becoming a working adult).
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.4.vi: I think studying diligently is a very good thing, but my opinion is somewhat different.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.4.grammar: Nominalization structure used to evaluate or comment on an action.
Shows concession before introducing a contrasting personal perspective.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.5.vi: Indeed, there are times when one feels that knowing English is convenient, such as when gathering overseas information on the Internet, while traveling abroad, or when asked for directions by foreign tourists even within Japan.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.5.grammar: Indeed... but... (conceding a point before introducing the primary counterargument).
During / throughout the period of an event.
Passive voice: '道を聞かれた' expresses being asked for directions.
The conjunctive adverb '確かに' (certainly / indeed) accompanies the concessive clause acknowledging the convenience of English ('feeling that English is convenient at times') before contrasting with the skeptical view in sentence 6 ('however, I question studying without purpose...'). Other connectors like 'その後' (after that), 'だから' (therefore), and 'すると' (upon which / then) cannot express this concessive-adversative relationship.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.6.vi: However, I feel doubtful about whether it is necessary to study without a purpose, simply for the reason that 'English is important.'
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.6.grammar: On the grounds that..., for the reason that...
There is a necessity to perform an action.
Sentence-final form providing explanatory weight or emphasizing personal convictions.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.7.vi: This is because, as long as one lives in Japan and works at a Japanese company, there are almost no opportunities where one must speak English.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.7.grammar: The reason is that... / This is because... (correlative pattern explaining the cause for the preceding statement).
As long as the prior condition persists, the following holds true.
Expresses obligation or necessity to do something.
The word 'なぜなら' (Because) at the beginning forms a complete correlative construction with 'からである' at the end ('なぜなら～からである': The reason is that...), directly explaining why the author expressed doubt in sentence 6. Other pairings such as 'ところが / にきまっている' (however / bound to be), 'ところで / わけである' (by the way / it means that), and 'なぜ / のだろうか' (why / could it be that - rhetorical question) do not provide a causal explanation for the preceding statement.
The predicate 'からである' at the end of the sentence combines with 'なぜなら' at the beginning to complete the causal grammatical structure 'なぜなら～からである' (The reason is that...).
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.8.vi: Many Japanese people also have few opportunities to associate with English speakers.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.8.grammar: Also have few opportunities to... (particle も adds an additional supporting reality).
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.9.vi: If so, for example, elementary schools should increase hours for studying Japanese, and company employees should study what is truly necessary for their respective jobs.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.9.grammar: Ought to / should do (expresses the speaker's recommendation or sensible proposition).
Based on the parallel suggestion structure '増やしたり、～(4)', the author advocates practical alternatives: elementary schools should increase Japanese instruction hours, and employees should learn what is truly necessary for their work ('学ぶべきだと思う' - I think they should study). Negative options such as Option 1 (thinking it is better not to study), Option 2 (not thinking it is good to study), and Option 3 (thinking one ought not to study) contradict the author's positive recommendation.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.10.vi: Wouldn't it be more beneficial to oneself to build Japanese proficiency and acquire immediately useful skills in this manner?
in that way / by doing so
wouldn't it be that... / isn't it true that
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.10.gramma: It is better / more advisable to do something.
To acquire, master, or internalize skills/knowledge.
Polite rhetorical phrasing used to strongly assert the author's viewpoint.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.sentences.10.keys.0: The phrase '( 5 ) 技術' connects directly to '仕事に本当に必要なこと' (what is genuinely necessary for work) mentioned in sentence 9. For working adults, acquiring skills that can be applied immediately to their daily duties ('すぐに役立つ' - immediately useful) provides far more personal benefit than studying English when one rarely has occasions to use it. Options such as 'いつか役立つ' (useful someday), 'ずっと役立たない' (never useful), and 'あまり役立たない' (rarely useful) fail to reflect the practical objective of meeting immediate job demands.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.outline.0.label: The current state of English education in Japan and the author's perspective
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.outline.0.note: The author raises the question of whether English is necessary, describes how widely English is studied from schools to workplaces, and presents their contrasting viewpoint.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.outline.1.label: Acknowledging English utility while questioning purposeless learning
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.outline.1.note: The author concedes that English can be useful at times, but questions learning without a clear purpose, since living and working in Japan rarely requires speaking English.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.outline.2.label: Proposal to prioritize Japanese and immediately applicable job skills
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.outline.2.note: The author suggests increasing Japanese instruction in elementary schools and recommends that working adults acquire practical skills that are immediately useful for their jobs.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t70-p1.vietnamese:
Is English education really necessary?
In Japan, people are often told that English education is of utmost importance. First of all, in schools, time is dedicated to learning English from elementary school all the way through high school. Furthermore, even after entering the workforce, a great many people attend English conversation classes or take various certification exams, either on their own initiative or at their company's instruction. While studying diligently is certainly commendable, my perspective is somewhat different.
Indeed, there are moments when one feels that understanding English is convenient, such as when gathering international information online, during overseas trips, or when asked for directions by foreign tourists while in Japan. However, I feel skeptical about whether there is truly a need to study English aimlessly, simply on the grounds that 'English is important.'
This is because, as long as one lives in Japan and works at a Japanese company, there are almost no occasions where speaking English is necessary. Most Japanese people also have few opportunities to interact with English speakers.
If that is the case, for instance, elementary schools should allocate more hours to learning Japanese, and company employees should study what is truly indispensable for their respective jobs. Wouldn't building proficiency in Japanese and acquiring immediately useful skills in this manner be far more beneficial to oneself?
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.sentences.0.vi: A recommendation to tour art museums
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.sentences.1.vi: This autumn, an art museum tour event is being held in the central area of City A.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.sentences.1.grammar: Marks a location as the setting or topic: in the central area of City A.
Describes an ongoing activity; here, the event is currently being held.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.sentences.2.vi: City A, which puts considerable effort into the arts, has three very famous art museums.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.sentences.2.grammar: To devote substantial effort to a field or activity.
A preceding clause modifies a noun: 芸術に力を入れている modifies A市.
States that something exists at a location presented as the topic.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.sentences.3.vi: In this event, participants visit three museums—the Prefectural Art Museum, the Municipal Art Museum, and the Yamada Tarō Memorial Art Museum—and receive a stamp on a sheet when entering each museum.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.sentences.3.grammar: The verb's masu-stem links actions in written language; まわり connects visiting the museums with receiving stamps.
Marks when an action occurs: receiving a stamp when entering a museum.
Explains the nature or procedure of the event just mentioned.
Question 2: stamps are obtained at individual museums, so the later reward condition concerns collecting stamps from at least two museums.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.sentences.4.vi: During the event, admission to any of the museums is 500 yen, regardless of age.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.sentences.4.grammar: Attaches to a period noun to mean 'during that period.'
どの美術館でも means 'at any of the museums,' without exception within the stated group.
The completion 年齢にかかわらず means the fee does not depend on age. ～にもかかわらず means 'despite' and does not fit this statement of a uniform fee.
Question 1: this announces a uniform admission fee; choose option 2, 年齢にかかわらず, meaning 'regardless of age.'
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.sentences.5.vi: The three museums are conveniently located within ten minutes of the station by train or bus.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.sentences.5.grammar: Expresses a condition: taking a train or bus makes it possible to arrive within the stated time.
Within the stated limit, including the limit itself; １０分以内 means no more than ten minutes.
Indicates the time needed to complete an action, here the journey to a museum.
行ける is the potential form of 行く; the preceding phrase modifies 場所 as a location one can reach.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.sentences.6.vi: If you collect stamps from at least two museums, you can receive one item of your choice from prizes such as picture postcards, posters, and stickers.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.sentences.6.grammar: At or above the stated quantity, including that quantity; ２館以上 means at least two museums.
集めると states a condition and its result under the event rules: collecting enough stamps qualifies you for a prize. ～とき marks a time and does not express this relationship appropriately.
Lists examples without implying that the list is exhaustive.
Indicates selection from a group: choosing one item from the available prizes.
もらえます is the polite potential form of もらう and directly states eligibility for a prize. もらえるようです means 'it seems you can receive one,' which is unsuitable for a direct announcement of the rules.
Question 2: the number of museums establishes a minimum requirement, calling for 集めると, 'if you collect the stamps.'
Question 2: the result is eligibility to receive one chosen prize, so もらえます fits. The complete pair is option 2.

default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.sentences.7.grammar: Adds information: special exhibitions are offered in addition to the stamp-collecting activity.

default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.sentences.9.vi: In particular, the Yamada Tarō Art Museum will display three paintings by Mr. Yamada Tarō that are not normally shown to the public and are regarded as masterpieces in the history of Japanese art.

default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.sentences.9.grammar: いつもは contrasts the paintings' usual lack of public display with their display on this occasion.
A negative passive form with ～ている; 公開されていない means 'are not publicly displayed.'
Highlights distinction within a broader scope; here, the paintings are recognized as masterpieces within Japanese art history.
Means 'is regarded as' or 'is considered to be,' expressing an established assessment.
Both 公開されていない and 「名作」とされている modify the paintings, rather than the museum or the artist.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.sentences.10.vi: The other museums also plan to display numerous famous paintings that everyone knows.
default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.sentences.10.gramma: Here, location-marking で combines with additive も: exhibitions will also take place at the other museums.
だれでも means 'anyone/everyone,' fitting widely known paintings. だれかが means 'someone'; だれかは does not express universality; だれにも does not fit 知っている in this construction.
知っている expresses the state of knowing something, rather than an action in progress.
いくつも in an affirmative clause emphasizes a large number.
A dictionary-form verb followed by 予定です expresses a plan. 展示される is passive, giving 'are scheduled to be exhibited.'

default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.sentences.11.gramma: Expresses a low degree: having little interest, rather than necessarily having none at all.
In the clause modifying 方, の in 関心のない can replace subject-marking が: people with little interest.
このような機会 means 'an opportunity like this,' referring to the event being introduced.
The masu-stem plus ながら expresses simultaneous activities: touring museums while enjoying an autumn of art.
Means to try doing something as an experience; 味わってみる means to try savoring it.
A polite suggestion meaning 'why not try...?' Complete it with いかがでしょうか. よろしいでしょうか tends to ask permission, while the two past-tense options do not fit a suggestion about a future experience.

default.p.chokuzen_n3-t72-p1.vietnamese:
A recommendation to tour art museums

This autumn, an art museum tour event is being held in the central area of City A. City A, which puts considerable effort into the arts, has three very famous art museums. In this event, participants visit three museums—the Prefectural Art Museum, the Municipal Art Museum, and the Yamada Tarō Memorial Art Museum—and receive a stamp on a sheet when entering each museum. During the event, admission to any of the museums is 500 yen, regardless of age. The three museums are conveniently located within ten minutes of the station by train or bus. If you collect stamps from at least two museums, you can receive one item of your choice from prizes such as picture postcards, posters, and stickers.

During the event, special exhibitions are also being held at all the museums. These exhibitions are also recommended. In particular, the Yamada Tarō Art Museum will display three paintings by Mr. Yamada Tarō that are not normally shown to the public and are regarded as masterpieces in the history of Japanese art. The other museums also plan to display numerous famous paintings that everyone knows.

Even if you have little interest in art or painting, why not take this opportunity to tour the museums and leisurely savor an 'autumn of art'?
